package.title: Flammability Test Method for Materials Intended for Use as Fire Barriers in Crewed Habitats
package.purpose: In some crewed-spacecraft applications, onboard materials are intentionally selected to function as hazard control barriers to prevent powered hardware and/or ignited flammable items from igniting nearby flammable materials by acting as non-breaching, non-flammable containment (e.g., cargo transfer bags, zero gravity stowage racks, and jettison stowage bags on the International Space Station). Historically, flammability self-extinguishment testing of broad acreage or outermost layer materials alone was believed to be sufficient to verify overall flammability compliance. Though required, testing on design features such as threaded seams and zippers was not performed due to the incorrect assumption that flammability performance would not be impacted. However, recent coupon level testing of layups and configurations consisting of multiple materials have revealed that these features may be more susceptible to ignition and fire propagation than the bulk material. Additionally, configurational coupon ignition and propagation testing does not explicitly determine a material’s ability to provide protection to vulnerable flammable hardware. The need to evaluate this gap in assessing material or layup effectiveness as fire barriers between ignition sources and flammable materials led to the development of a new configuration-based fire barrier test. Test setup, relevant configurations, and test validation are discussed. The new barrier test method establishes a configuration for the test apparatus, identifies a conservative ignitor configuration, and defines pass/fail criteria. Test setup, relevant configurations, and test validation are discussed.

In some crewed-spacecraft applications, onboard materials are intentionally selected to 
function as hazard control barriers to prevent powered hardware and/or ignited flammable 
items from igniting nearby flammable materials by acting as non-breaching, non-flammable 
containment (e.g., cargo transfer bags, zero gravity stowage racks, and jettison stowage bags 
on the International Space Station). Historically, flammability self-extinguishment testing of 
broad acreage or outermost layer materials alone was believed to be sufficient to verify overall 
flammability compliance. Though required, testing on design features such as threaded seams 
and zippers was not performed due to the incorrect assumption that flammability 
performance would not be impacted. However, recent coupon level testing of layups and 
configurations consisting of multiple materials have revealed that these features may be more 
susceptible to ignition and fire propagation than the bulk material. Additionally, 
configurational coupon ignition and propagation testing does not explicitly determine a 
material’s ability to provide protection to vulnerable flammable hardware.  The need to 
evaluate this gap in assessing material or layup effectiveness as fire barriers between ignition 
sources and flammable materials led to the development of a new configuration-based fire 
barrier test. Test setup, relevant configurations, and test validation are discussed. The new 
barrier test method establishes a configuration for the test apparatus, identifies a conservative 
ignitor configuration, and defines pass/fail criteria. Test setup, relevant configurations, and 
test validation are discussed.

I. Introduction 
PACECRAFT intended for crewed spaceflight must maintain environments that support human survival and 
enable the operational requirements of their mission. Further, spacecraft must be designed to protect inhabitants 
from nominal space environments as well as off-nominal scenarios arising from emergency events. One such 
emergency event is fire within a spacecraft. The catastrophic events of 1967 in which astronauts Virgil ‘Gus’ Grissom, 
Edward H. White, II, and Roger B. Chafee were tragically killed during an Apollo 1 ground test led to significant 
investigation and changes to how NASA approaches spacecraft fire safety. The overarching three-pronged approach 
is still in use by NASA today and includes a combination of controlling ignition sources, selecting materials that are 
self-extinguishing in the cabin environment, and general fire mitigation. This approach does not prohibit materials 
that can ignite but does seek to prevent propagation of fire when ignition occurs. The predominant material 
propagation test employed by NASA is outlined in NASA Standard 6001 (NASA-STD-6001) Test 1. [1] In this test, 
a material is placed in a vertical configuration with its lower edge near an ignitor designed [2] to provide energy for 
25 + 5 seconds (s).  If the material burns at least 6 inches (~3 inches beyond the ignitor affected zone), it is deemed a 
failure, indicating that it could propagate if ignited in a spacecraft. The testing is performed in an enclosed chamber 
with the starting environment mimicking the cabin environment.  
For the materials that are known to propagate when evaluated under NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, but are sufficiently 
critical, exceptions for use are made based on accepted configurations and use application. For example, personal 
hygiene wipes and paper cue cards are known to fail Test 1 in cabin environments, but they are given an exception 
from meeting requirements if they are in use, staged away from powered hardware, or stored in containers that serve 
as a barrier between any ignition source and the flammable materials. Another example is the construction of acoustic 
panels used on walls of spacecraft. Flammable foams and battings perform well as acoustic dampeners but are 
combined with non-propagating textiles to serve as a barrier between potential ignition sources and the flammable 
foam. These ‘barrier materials’ such as cargo transfer bags and large area layups such as acoustic panels have 
historically been evaluated using Test 1 to assess each individual material. However, recent unpublished testing in 
large-scale applications has revealed that a material passing ignition resistance testing does not guarantee barrier 
performance against larger than 25-second ignition challenges. 
There is an understanding that the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 ignitor is intended to bound most electrical failure 
ignition scenarios. However, recent testing has shed light on the fact that propagation performance when exposed to 
Test 1 ignitor energy is vastly different from propagation performance when exposed to a much larger ignition energy, 
such as a kindling chain reaction or lithium-ion battery thermal runaway event. Despite great efforts made to select 
non-flammable materials for vehicle design, there are still small amounts of known flammables that must be used in 
vehicles. The goal is to minimize use of known flammables needed for everyday life and operations (e.g., crew 
clothing, paper, post-it notes, and hook and loop fasteners) while ensuring major design materials are self-
extinguishing if ignited. Nonetheless, these known flammables when ignited could pose a greater than 25-second 
ignition risk to other cabin materials and barriers. Additionally, though the likelihood of a battery cell undergoing 
thermal runaway is very low, it is important that a barrier test aimed at proving a material or layup’s ability to protect 
from ignition is sufficiently conservative, bounding these ignition energy and duration scenarios. 
Configuration control against ignition sources can be achieved via design and spacing in unmanned spacecraft, 
crew inaccessible areas, and enclosed oxygen systems. However, the introduction of astronauts in the loop opens the 
door to lack of configuration control and a multitude of scenarios that could not have been imagined. Despite 
operational control guidance, years of human spaceflight experience have demonstrated that crew habitability needs 
drive material configurations beyond those assessed on the ground. These adaptations — while understandable and 
often necessary for crew performance and wellbeing — can result in significant uncontrolled flammable material 
accumulation, including large hook and loop fields, repurposed polyethylene bags, and incidental soft goods, creating 
propagation paths not present in the baseline configuration. Configuration changes in real-time means that known

cabin flammables (e.g., clothing, paper, post it notes, and hook and loop fasteners) could potentially encounter primary 
ignition sources, ignite, and become much larger secondary ignition sources within the cabin. Furthermore, in this 
evaluation, battery fires and commonly used cabin known flammables, were characterized as ignition sources. 
Additionally, construction and design features, such as thread patterns and zippers, can introduce weaknesses that 
allow for propagation despite the presence of the barrier material and were also evaluated in this study. 
 
The observations from the large-scale test, as well as the development work done on exploration atmosphere cargo 
transfer bags, prompted development of a new standardized test method to evaluate the effectiveness of barrier 
materials to not only self-extinguish but to prevent breach and therefore protect enclosed flammables. The 
development effort sought to define the critical parameters required for a standardized test along with pass/fail criteria. 
Development effort included three parts: testing and development of an ignitor to mimic reasonable cabin ignition 
sources, development of a standardized barrier test configuration, and development of pass/fail criteria. Here we 
describe the process and results of the Barrier Test Method development.  
II. Barrier Test Development 
A. Exploratory Barrier Testing 
The overarching role of barrier materials is to protect 
ignitable and propagating materials from primary or secondary 
ignition sources such as known cabin flammables. The general 
approach was to develop a test that allowed the barrier material 
to be placed between the ignitor and ‘challenge materials’ (i.e., 
common cabin materials known to be highly ignitable and 
propagating). The first design of a barrier test apparatus is 
shown in Figure 1. In this design, the barrier material was 
placed perpendicular to the flame, and the challenge material 
was placed with the raw edge in direct contact with the barrier 
material. These first tests attempted to use known possible 
secondary ignition sources, such as cotton socks, as the ignition 
source for the test. The concept was to ignite the known cabin 
flammable and observe the barrier and challenge material 
performance. If the barrier material were to be breached by the 
flame or if the temperature across the barrier material was high 
enough to ignite the challenge material, then the barrier material 
would fail. However, if the barrier material was not breached 
and the challenge material did not propagate, then the barrier 
material would pass.  
Two issues with the early approach were identified and 
resulted in significant deviations from the original plan. First, using actual known cabin flammables did not provide a 
repeatable and consistent energy level and burn duration between tests. For this reason, the team determined that using 
standard ignitors would provide more repeatable results if they could identify an ignitor configuration that bounded 
known flammable materials for energy and duration. The results of the effort to develop this ignitor are described in 
section B below. Second, some of the barrier materials tested were shown to ‘draw away’ from the edges of the sample 
holder, resulting in breaches of the material around the edge. Several design iterations were attempted, but concerns 
remained. Breaches were observed not caused by flame burn through but by the test fixture design wherein heating of 
the material was causing sufficient stress along the edges to induce breaching. Accordingly, the team took a new test 
fixture and sample set up approach that removed heat shrink stresses as a variable impacting results and expanded the 
capabilities of the test to evaluate full barrier layups and their design features. The details of the test development are 
described in section C below.  
B. Ignitor Development 
The ignitor is a key component in flammability and ignition resistance testing for spacecraft materials. It serves as 
a controlled ignition source to evaluate whether materials ignite and propagate flames under specific oxygen 
concentrations and configurations per NASA-STD-6001. Historically, the 25-second burn Test 1 ignitor was selected 
as a robust ignition challenge for screening materials after the Apollo 1 fire. It provides a high-energy, long-duration

and consistent flame. The intent was to ensure a material’s edge ignition and assess self-extinguishment, not to directly 
replicate real-world ignition sources.  
 
As the cabin environments considered for exploration missions increase above the terrestrial nominal of 21% 
oxygen, fewer materials are available that pass NASA-STD-6001. Accordingly, more consideration must be given to 
known cabin flammable secondary ignition sources such as burning hook and loop fasteners, paper, or clothing, which 
can exceed Test 1 ignitor energy and duration. Additionally, lithium ion (Li-ion) batteries were not a recognized risk 
following Apollo. These batteries generate considerably more energy than a Test 1 ignitor and are used broadly in 
cabin hardware such as laptop computers, cameras, etc. In summary, the 25-second Test 1 ignitor does not bound 
worst case ignition sources or known flammable secondary ignition sources when barrier protection of flammables is 
the goal.  To address these concerns, testing was conducted on a series of materials known to be used widely in the 
spacecraft cabin environment. A thermocouple was placed within the hottest location of the flame to measure 
temperature as a function of time. Materials tested included:

D. Pass/Fail Criteria Development 
 
The next phase of the effort consisted of defining verifiable, repeatable, and rigorous Pass/Fail criteria. Statistical 
analysis of NASA’s Materials and Processes Technical Information Systems (MAPTIS) database [5] for Test 1 data 
was conducted to determine the appropriate number of replicates needed for precision and confidence in the test 
process and results. Data were analyzed from more than 30,000 historical tests conducted on materials in 19 categories. 
The uncertainty in the burn length was calculated using a 95% confidence upper bound as a function of sample size 
and standard deviation as shown in Figure 9. Consider a sample size of 5 and a standard deviation of 3 inches (indicated 
by the purple curve), then an upper bound on the burn length is calculated as the mean + 2.9 inches. Figure 9 shows 
that as the number of replicates increases, the uncertainty decreases; however, there is a point of diminishing returns 
where additional replicates provide little benefit. Approximately half the cases in the MAPTIS Test 1 data had a burn 
length standard deviation less than 3 inches, while the other half of the cases had a standard deviation between 3 and 
6.5 inches. Based on these results and the curves in Figure 9, a baseline of 5 replicates was determined to be sufficient 
for the new barrier test. However, if the standard deviation of the challenge material heat affected length is greater 
than 3 inches, then the number of replicates is increased from 5 to 10 to reduce uncertainty.

IV. Final Test Configuration and Pass/Fail Criteria 
 
The final test configuration, as shown in Figure 13, was reported via Technical Memo [6] from NASA’s 
Engineering and Safety Center. Key design specifications include the test fixture which is large to eliminate the edge 
effects observed in the exploratory testing. The final size is 12” (30.5cm) width x 24” (61cm) length. The ‘L’ portion 
of the L-configuration is controlled at a 1” bend radius. Final challenge materials are sheets of 0.004” (0.01cm) thick 
polyethylene and 0.01” (0.03cm) thick cellulosic dry 
wipes due to their worst-case AITs. Each is installed in a 
dedicated frame and cut along the lower edge to have ½” 
(1.27cm) wide, 1.5” (3.81cm) long slits. The slitted 
portions of the challenge materials are placed in contact 
with horizontal portion of the barrier material with a 5/8” 
(1.59cm) gap between each material. The dry wipe is 
placed nearest to the barrier material. The simulated 
single-cell battery failure ignitor is placed ¼” (0.64cm) 
below the barrier material during testing. Five replicates 
are completed of the test for a given material 
layup/configuration.  
 
Three conditions were defined that can result in an 
immediate Fail: 
1. Full upward propagation of one or more of the 
barrier layup materials 
2. Sustained combustion of one or both challenge 
materials 
3. Burn-through (breach) hole observable with the 
naked eye post-test. 
Note that these conditions apply to any single test of the 
five replicates. If one out of five tests resulted in a failure, 
then the material layup fails. In some tests, charring was 
observed on the challenge materials that did not result in 
full propagation. Based on the statistical analysis to 
determine confidence in five replicates demonstrating a 
failing layup, the following criteria were applied to charring of the barrier and challenge materials: 
• 
If length of charring (of any one sample – across 5 initial replicates) on the interior of the barrier is >3” 
(7.62cm) away from the ignitor impingement point, run 5 additional replicates 
• 
If the standard deviation (between the 5 initial replicates) of the challenge material heat affected lengths is 
>3” (7.62cm), run 5 additional replicates 
A failure (per #1-3 above) of any of the 5 additional replicates would result in a Fail. However, if the data from the 5 
additional replicates does not decisively fail but continues to show large or highly varied heat affected areas, the data 
are used to inform the risk of the design. 
V. Conclusion 
A new standardized test method has been developed to evaluate materials intended for use as flammability barriers 
between potential ignition sources and known flammable and propagating materials. Future work will include testing 
of additional materials to build the database of barrier material performance, performing testing at multiple labs to 
assess reproducibility, as well as incorporation of the test method into NASA-STD-6001 and implementation across 
NASA programs, where needed.  
Acknowledgments 
The authors would like to acknowledge the test team at WSTF who made this testing possible as well as NASA’s 
Engineering and Safety Center for funding this development.  
 
 
Figure 13. Final Barrier Test Configuration.

metadata.title: Flammability Test Method for Materials Intended for Use as Fire Barriers in Crewed Habitats
metadata.abstract: In some crewed-spacecraft applications, onboard materials are intentionally selected to function as hazard control barriers to prevent powered hardware and/or ignited flammable items from igniting nearby flammable materials by acting as non-breaching, non-flammable containment (e.g., cargo transfer bags, zero gravity stowage racks, and jettison stowage bags on the International Space Station). Historically, flammability self-extinguishment testing of broad acreage or outermost layer materials alone was believed to be sufficient to verify overall flammability compliance. Though required, testing on design features such as threaded seams and zippers was not performed due to the incorrect assumption that flammability performance would not be impacted. However, recent coupon level testing of layups and configurations consisting of multiple materials have revealed that these features may be more susceptible to ignition and fire propagation than the bulk material. Additionally, configurational coupon ignition and propagation testing does not explicitly determine a material’s ability to provide protection to vulnerable flammable hardware. The need to evaluate this gap in assessing material or layup effectiveness as fire barriers between ignition sources and flammable materials led to the development of a new configuration-based fire barrier test. Test setup, relevant configurations, and test validation are discussed. The new barrier test method establishes a configuration for the test apparatus, identifies a conservative ignitor configuration, and defines pass/fail criteria. Test setup, relevant configurations, and test validation are discussed.
